problem: The failure condition is wrong. With 24 vCPU configured on 8 physical cores, contention does not start when combined demand approaches 24 cores; the host only has 8 cores of real capacity, so queues build once the VMs' combined busy vCPU demand approaches 8 cores. Saying it fails only near 24 cores would make overcommit look far safer than it is.
fix: The 24 vCPU are limits, not reserved cores. The hypervisor schedules them onto 8 cores and relies on most VMs being idle. It fails when the combined busy demand of the VMs approaches the host's real capacity of 8 cores: run queues grow, every guest slows down and latency rises.

problem: Cores and vCPU are mixed in one subtraction (16 cores - 10 vCPU), which reads as if the two units were interchangeable, the very confusion the exam traps warn against.
fix: Allocated vCPU limit = 10 vCPU out of a hosting capacity of 16 cores, so the unused vCPU allowance is 16 - 10 = 6 vCPU (assuming one vCPU per core here).

problem: The text states flatly that the hypervisor sits on the hardware and owns the real hardware. That is true only for bare-metal (Type 1) hypervisors; a hosted (Type 2) hypervisor runs as a program on top of an ordinary host OS.
fix: A hypervisor is the software layer that creates and runs VMs. A bare-metal (Type 1) hypervisor sits directly on the hardware and owns it; a hosted (Type 2) hypervisor runs as a program on top of a normal host OS. Designs differ; see 3.3.

problem: Ten old servers each at 10% CPU add up to about one full server of CPU demand. If the new host is the size of one old server, the example leaves no headroom and contradicts the claim of a comfortable consolidation. It works only if the receiving host is larger than any single old server.
fix: Ten old servers, each using a small fraction of its own much larger capacity, become ten VMs on one powerful host, with less power, cooling, rack space and cabling.

problem: The sentence 'Everything about the VM travels in those files' clashes with the live-migration answer in Q3, where the running memory state is copied over the network, not carried in the VM's files.
fix: A VM's configuration and disks live in a small set of files, plus a memory snapshot if one is taken; when a running VM is migrated, its memory pages are transferred separately to the new host.
